summary: A yes/no question keeps the word order of the statement. In speech the voice simply rises at the end: אַתָּה רוֹצֶה קָפֶה? “Do you want coffee?” — in writing the question mark shows it. Formal and written Hebrew may open the question with הַאִם: הַאִם אַתָּה רוֹצֶה קָפֶה? There is no inversion and no auxiliary verb. Answer with כֵּן “yes” or לֹא “no” — or, very often, by repeating the verb: — אַתָּה רוֹצֶה? — רוֹצֶה! Useful replies: כַּמּוּבָן or בָּרוּר “of course”, אוּלַי “maybe”, בֶּאֱמֶת? “really?”, גַּם אֲנִי “me too”, רַק … “only …”. A choice question uses אוֹ “or”: תֵּה אוֹ קָפֶה? — and is answered with one of the choices, not with yes or no. To contradict a negative question (German doch), say the verb again or דַּוְקָא כֵּן “actually, yes”: — אַתָּה לֹא רוֹצֶה? — דַּוְקָא כֵּן!

blocks.title: Your voice is the grammar
blocks.text: Hebrew changes nothing in the sentence: no inversion, no “do”, no particle in everyday speech. The rising voice — and in writing the question mark — turns a statement into a question.

blocks.title: A choice: אוֹ
blocks.text: תֵּה אוֹ קָפֶה? asks “which one?”: the voice rises on תֵּה and falls on קָפֶה, and the answer is one of them — not כֵּן or לֹא.

blocks.title: הַאִם is not אִם
blocks.text: הַאִם opens a question (formal); אִם alone means “if”. In conversation הַאִם can sound stiff — leave it out.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Everyday or formal? (voice only, or הַאִם)
Did I keep the statement order?
Is it a choice with אוֹ? (then it is not a yes/no question)

askYourself: Is it everyday speech? → keep the statement and raise your voice at the end (write “?”).
Is it formal or written? → put הַאִם at the very beginning.
Did I change the word order? → don’t: Hebrew questions keep the statement order.
Do I need a word for “do / does”? → no, Hebrew has none.
Is it a choice between two things? → use אוֹ; the answer is one of them.
Answering a negative question with “yes, I do”? → repeat the verb or say דַּוְקָא כֵּן.
steps: Raise the voice at the end (or open with הַאִם).
Answer with כֵּן / לֹא, or repeat the verb.

traps: No inversion and no “do”: “Do you want tea?” = אַתָּה רוֹצֶה תֵּה?
הַאִם is formal; in conversation it can sound stiff.
Do not confuse הַאִם (question particle) with אִם (“if”).
A question by intonation alone shows in writing only by its question mark — don’t forget it.
A choice question with אוֹ is not answered with כֵּן / לֹא, but with one of the choices.
To a negative question, a bare כֵּן is unclear — repeat the verb or say דַּוְקָא כֵּן.

quiz.q: How do you turn אַתָּה שׁוֹתֶה תֵּה into a question in everyday speech?
options: raise the voice at the end: אַתָּה שׁוֹתֶה תֵּה?
put the verb first: שׁוֹתֶה אַתָּה תֵּה?
quiz.answer: raise the voice at the end: אַתָּה שׁוֹתֶה תֵּה?
quiz.why: Hebrew keeps the statement order and has no “do”; intonation (and the question mark) makes the question.

quiz.q: Which word opens a yes/no question in formal Hebrew?
quiz.why: הַאִם is the question particle; אִם alone means “if”, and אוֹ means “or”.

quiz.q: Someone asks אַתָּה לֹא רוֹצֶה קָפֶה? — but you do want some. What do you answer?
quiz.why: Hebrew has no “doch”: you contradict the “not” by repeating the verb or with דַּוְקָא כֵּן “actually, yes”.

quiz.q: תֵּה אוֹ קָפֶה? — what kind of answer does it expect?
options: one of the two: תֵּה or קָפֶה
quiz.answer: one of the two: תֵּה or קָפֶה
quiz.why: With אוֹ it is a choice question, not a yes/no question.

seeAlso.note: Arabic opens a yes/no question with هَلْ or أَ — the counterpart of the formal הַאִם; in everyday Arabic intonation alone is also common.
German puts the verb first (Willst du …?) and answers a negative question with doch; Hebrew keeps the statement order and says דַּוְקָא כֵּן.
Chinese adds 吗 at the end or asks A-not-A (要不要); its choice questions use 还是 — Hebrew uses intonation or הַאִם, and אוֹ for a choice.

notes.text: As in Russian, intonation alone makes the question (Ты хочешь кофе? ~ אַתָּה רוֹצֶה קָפֶה?). The formal הַאִם is a little like ли, but it always stands first.
As in Greek, the word order stays and only the voice rises (Θέλεις καφέ; ~ אַתָּה רוֹצֶה קָפֶה?). Hebrew writes the question mark ?, not ;.
As in Spanish, intonation alone turns a statement into a question (¿Quieres café? ~ אַתָּה רוֹצֶה קָפֶה?); Hebrew writes only the final question mark.
English inverts or uses “do”; Hebrew changes nothing: “Do you want coffee?” = אַתָּה רוֹצֶה קָפֶה?
As in spoken French (tu veux du café ?), intonation is enough; formal הַאִם at the start plays the part of est-ce que.
German moves the verb to the front (Willst du Kaffee?); Hebrew keeps the statement order. For doch, Hebrew repeats the verb or says דַּוְקָא כֵּן.
Hindi may open a yes/no question with क्या or rely on intonation alone; Hebrew הַאִם works the same way, but it is formal.
Persian آیا at the start is optional and formal, like הַאִם; in speech intonation alone does it, in both languages.
Marathi often adds का at the end (तू येणार आहेस का?); Hebrew puts its optional particle at the start (הַאִם) and in speech usually uses none.
Arabic opens a question with هَلْ or أَ; Hebrew הַאִם is the formal counterpart, and everyday Hebrew drops it and uses intonation.
Turkish adds the particle mi after the word in question (Kahve istiyor musun?); Hebrew adds nothing in speech — formal הַאִם goes at the start.
Japanese ends a question with か (コーヒーを飲みますか); Hebrew uses only the voice, or formal הַאִם at the start.
Korean marks a question with the verb ending and intonation (커피 마셔요?); Hebrew changes no ending — the voice alone does it.
Finnish adds -ko / -kö to the first word and moves it to the front (Haluatko kahvia?); Hebrew keeps the order and adds nothing.
As in Hungarian (Kávét kérsz?), a yes/no question keeps the order and uses intonation; formal Hebrew can add הַאִם at the start.
Swahili also uses intonation (unataka kahawa?) and may open with je, as Hebrew may with הַאִם.
Chinese ends with 吗 or uses verb-不-verb (你要不要咖啡?); Hebrew needs neither — the rising voice alone, or formal הַאִם at the start. As in Chinese, a short “yes” can repeat the verb: — רוֹצֶה!
Vietnamese frames the question with có … không (anh có muốn cà phê không?); Hebrew uses only the rising voice, or formal הַאִם at the start.
Inuktitut marks a question with an interrogative verb ending (such as -vit “you?”); Hebrew leaves the verb as it is and uses intonation.
